summary: Records an agreement between Sun Microsystems and the Internet Society allowing Sun's Network File System specifications to enter the IETF standards process, covering the NFS version 4 work.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2339 records an agreement between Sun Microsystems and the Internet Society about developing NFS Version 4 through the IETF standards process. Sun grants rights to use and modify the specifications for that purpose, with a 24-month condition for the evolution license.

questions: what is the 24 month limit in the nfs agreement
subtitle: The agreement that allowed Sun's NFS specifications to enter the IETF standards process.

tldr.problem: The IETF needed permission to use and modify Sun's NFS specifications while developing a specification for NFS Version 4 through the Internet standards process.
tldr.mechanism: Sun granted the Internet Society and the IETF a cost-free, worldwide, non-exclusive license to use and modify the specification for the sole purpose of seeking an Internet standard.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2339 records the agreement and is not itself a standard. The evolution license terminates if the specification does not reach Proposed Standard within 24 months of signing.

today: RFC 2339 is an Informational record of an agreement, and the unit metadata lists no RFC as obsoleting or updating it. The RFC is not a technical standard.

sections.title: What the Agreement Covers
sections.content:
RFC 2339 is an official public record of an agreement between Sun Microsystems and the Internet Society, made on 3 March 1998. The agreement permits Sun's Network File System specifications to enter the Internet standards process conducted by the IETF. The RFC explicitly says it is not a standard.

The agreement incorporates RFC 1094 and RFC 1813 by reference as source specifications. It also addresses control of ONC RPC program number 100003 for generating NFS version numbers 4 and onward.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC publishes a legal agreement that lets Sun's NFS specifications be used as the starting point for IETF work on NFS Version 4. It records permission and conditions, not a new NFS protocol.

sections.title: Rights Granted to the Internet Society and IETF
sections.content:
Sun grants the Internet Society and the IETF a cost-free, perpetual, non-exclusive, worldwide license under specified Sun copyrights, essential patent rights, and other intellectual property rights. The license allows them to use, reproduce, distribute, perform, display, and create derivative works from the specification, and to authorize others to do so.

The license is limited to seeking to make the specification an Internet standard. Sun also grants the licensees the right to evolve, develop, and modify the specification through the Internet Standardization Process. Sun agrees not to license another party to evolve or promote it as a standard, and says development outside that process must be identified as non-standard.
sections.plainLanguage: The agreement lets the Internet Society and IETF use and change the NFS specification for work toward an Internet standard. It does not grant those rights for unrelated purposes.

sections.title: The 24-Month Condition
sections.content:
The licensees have no duty to publish the specification or advance it onto the standards track, and they have no confidentiality obligation. Sun agrees to license the specification to others at no charge on substantially similar terms if it reaches Proposed Standard within 24 months of the agreement, provided those licensees implement and comply with the standard.

If the specification does not reach Proposed Standard within 24 months of the agreement, the license to evolve, develop, and modify it under Section 3 terminates. The RFC also states that rights not expressly granted are reserved by Sun.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF does not have to publish or standardize the specification. But if it reaches Proposed Standard within 24 months, Sun agrees to offer others a no-charge license on similar terms; otherwise, the evolution license ends.

sections.title: Other Terms and Security
sections.content: The agreement provides the specification “as is,” disclaims warranties, and limits Sun's liability. It also sets terms for written changes, export-control compliance, and applicable law. The RFC says security is not directly affected because it records an agreement rather than describing technology, while stating that an IETF NFS working group should aim for adequate security in a standards-track NFS protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The document includes legal terms about warranties, liability, and changes to the agreement. It says the agreement itself does not directly affect security, but an NFS standard should have adequate security.
